Whose Credential Is It? How Owner Attribution in Agent Memory
Shapes Cross-User Account Misuse

Hau-Sing So ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: University of Macau    Daixian Liu11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Carl Hou Affiliation: Lanzhou University    Yuhaohang He Affiliation: Sichuan Agricultural University    Mengzhu Wang Affiliation: Hebei University of Technology    Hai-Tao Zheng ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Tsinghua University
Abstract

Shared long-term memory lets an LLM agent serving one user inadvertently retrieve another user’s credentials, but it is unclear when such exposure leads to actual harm. We introduce a three-stage audit that separates three events: a foreign credential reaches the prompt (exposure), the agent acts with it (behavior), and the other user’s account changes (state). In AppWorld, a store that mixes 763 past logins from all users retrieves another user’s credential for 84.7% of required apps, yet agents rarely act on it. Misuse appears in a stress test where memory lacks the user’s own credential and presents a single foreign one as the user’s record: seven agents then use it in 80–94% of runs and change the victim’s account in up to 43%, sometimes passing the official check. Naming the owner before or inside each credential line prevents most of this: with all else fixed, misuse falls from 92 to 1 of 305 paired runs, also with name-free usernames, though owner-bound notes cost 3–5 successful tasks per model on clean memory. A wrongly written owner largely restores misuse; trailing owner tags and added safety instructions help only some models. Agent memory should consistently record whose credential it stores, and evaluations should measure behavior, not only exposure.

1 Introduction

Long-term memory turns a stateless language model into an assistant that remembers procedures, preferences and the account details it needs to act (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Chhikara et al., 2025). Deployed assistants serve many people, and their memories are pooled, consolidated or indexed together (Rezazadeh et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a). A note written while serving Alice can then be retrieved while serving Bob. If the note holds Alice’s password, the agent becomes a confused deputy (Hardy, 1988): it holds authority granted by one person and may use it for another. Unlike prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024) or memory poisoning (Chen et al., 2024), this needs no attacker (Figure 1).

Whether such a mistake causes harm depends on three separate events. A foreign credential must first reach the prompt (exposure, a property of the store and the retriever); the agent must then use it (behavior, a property of the model and of how memory is worded); finally, the other user’s account must change (state). Existing evaluations usually observe one end of this chain: whether contaminated content reaches or steers the agent (Yang et al., 2026b; Cerruti et al., 2026), or whether the task succeeds (Trivedi et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024). Judged on exposure alone, almost every shared store looks unsafe; judged on task success alone, actions in the wrong account go unnoticed. As a result, it is unclear when exposure becomes harm and what designers can do about it.

We make this chain measurable in AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), a stateful environment with 99 users whose accounts can be logged into and modified. We label the account behind every API call and audit the other user’s account between checkpoints. We first measure how often a shared store exposes another user’s credential and how often agents act on it. We then run a controlled stress test: a valid foreign credential is fixed while only its wording varies, across seven models and two disjoint task cohorts, followed by controls whose designs were fixed before they were run. The main finding is that whether exposure becomes harm depends largely on one property of memory text that designers control: whether each credential is tied to its owner (Table 1). We treat owner wording as a second layer behind access control, not as a replacement for it. Our contributions are:

  • •

    An audit that separates exposure, behavior and state through an exposure census, per-call identity labeling and a read-only audit of the victim’s account. It shows that success-only evaluation misses harm: 29 runs passed the official check while using another user’s token.

  • •

    Evidence that exposure is a poor proxy for harm. Agents act on foreign credentials mainly when memory lacks the user’s own credential for an app and offers a single foreign one worded as the user’s record; with the user’s own credential also present, misuse nearly disappears.

  • •

    Evidence that owner attribution is an effective write-time lever. Naming owners lowers misuse from 92 to 1 of 305 paired runs and remains effective with phone-number usernames, with paraphrases, and when only the foreign line is named. A wrongly written owner restores much of the misuse, so the owner must come from an authenticated source.

2 Related Work

Agent Memory

Memory architectures store and retrieve interaction history (Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Chhikara et al., 2025), and benchmarks evaluate recall over long dialogues (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024a). Both largely assume a single user. Memory can also leak private data to attackers (Wang et al., 2025); we instead study a benign flow of authority to the wrong person.

Multiple Principals and Authority

Benign interactions contaminate shared agent state (Yang et al., 2026b), and agents serving several users fail to keep their interests and privacy apart (Yang et al., 2026a). Consolidation can erase a memory’s original source authority (Zhan et al., 2026) or turn unverified hearsay into seemingly confident facts (Kwon, 2026), and Cerruti et al. (2026) separate how fabricated permissions enter memory from whether an executor acts on them. Proposed defenses include access control for shared memory (Rezazadeh et al., 2025), provenance firewalls and origin-bound authority (Xu et al., 2026; Louck, 2026), capability tracking (Debenedetti et al., 2026), information-flow control (Costa et al., 2025) and execution isolation (Wu et al., 2024b). Our study differs in four ways: the credentials are valid rather than fabricated, every call is labeled with the account it acts in, the victim’s account state is audited, and only the wording of a fixed credential is varied. Wording is a write-time lever that complements these controls, unlike poisoned content (Chen et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025).

Privacy, Safety and Prompt Form

Contextual integrity (Nissenbaum, 2004) has been probed in LLM conversations (Mireshghallah et al., 2024) and agent actions (Shao et al., 2024). Agent safety suites test injected instructions and risky tool use (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024; Levy et al., 2026; Jia et al., 2025). Marking provenance in prompts defends against injection (Hines et al., 2024), and LLMs are sensitive to prompt format (Sclar et al., 2024), instruction provenance (Wallace et al., 2024) and how entities are bound in context (Feng and Steinhardt, 2024). We show that how memory text attaches an owner to a credential shapes a security-relevant action.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Setting

Figure 2 summarizes the audit. Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be a set of users and 𝒜\mathcal{A} a set of apps. Each account (u,a)(u,a) is protected by a credential κu,a\kappa_{u,a}. A task τ\tau is issued by a requester r⁡(τ)∈𝒰r(\tau)\in\mathcal{U} (AppWorld’s “supervisor”) and requires apps A⁡(τ)⊆𝒜A(\tau)\subseteq\mathcal{A}. A shared store ℳ={mi}\mathcal{M}=\{m_{i}\} holds notes m=(om,am,κm)m=(o_{m},a_{m},\kappa_{m}), each with an owner, an app and a credential. A retriever returns the top-kk notes ℛk​(τ)≡ℛk​(qτ,ℳ)\mathcal{R}_{k}(\tau)\equiv\mathcal{R}_{k}(q_{\tau},\mathcal{M}) for a query qτq_{\tau}. A renderer ρ\rho turns them into text, and the agent πθ\pi_{\theta} receives

Pτ=[I;λ​ℓr⁡(τ);ρ⁡(ℛk​(τ));xτ],P_{\tau}=\big[\,I;\ \lambda\,\ell_{r(\tau)};\ \rho\big(\mathcal{R}_{k}(\tau)\big);\ x_{\tau}\,\big], (1)

where II is the agent instruction and xτx_{\tau} the task. The requester line ℓr\ell_{r} (“My name is …”) precedes every AppWorld task; λ∈{0,1}\lambda\in\{0,1\} toggles it. The agent emits API calls ξ=(c1,…,cT)\xi=(c_{1},\dots,c_{T}). We write id⁡(ct)∈𝒰∪{⊥}\mathrm{id}(c_{t})\in\mathcal{U}\cup\{\bot\} for the user whose session token a call carries (⊥\bot if none). The donor dd (the victim) is the user whose credential is exposed.

No party is adversarial: memory is written from real sessions, and the failure is using valid authority for the wrong person. Owner information is usually available at write time, because the agent knows whom it is serving; keeping it in the memory text is a design choice. The intended behavior is to act only in the requester’s account: use a stored credential only if it is the requester’s, and otherwise obtain the requester’s own through the supervisor API (AppWorld offers no channel to ask the user). Authorized delegation is outside our scope.

3.2 Exposure, Behavior and State

Exposure

A required app a∈A⁡(τ)a\in A(\tau) is exposed when the prompt contains another user’s credential for it:

𝖤⁡(τ,a)=maxm∈ℛk​(τ)⁡𝕀⁡[am=a,om≠r⁡(τ)].\mathsf{E}(\tau,a)=\max_{m\in\mathcal{R}_{k}(\tau)}\mathbb{I}\big[a_{m}{=}a,\ o_{m}{\neq}r(\tau)\big]. (2)

The census reports the app-level rate 𝖤¯app\bar{\mathsf{E}}_{\text{app}}, the mean over all pairs (τ,a)(\tau,a) with a∈A⁡(τ)a\in A(\tau); no model call is needed. A run is exposed if its prompt contains any foreign credential.

Behavior

A run exhibits misuse when any call acts in another person’s account:

𝖡(ξ)=𝕀[∃t:id(ct)∉{r(τ),⊥}].\mathsf{B}(\xi)=\mathbb{I}\big[\exists\,t:\ \mathrm{id}(c_{t})\notin\{r(\tau),\bot\}\big]. (3)

We decode the token subject (app+username) of every call and map usernames to people via the 99 users’ login histories. 𝖡\mathsf{B}, a wrong-token run, is our primary endpoint. A looser endpoint, 𝖡login\mathsf{B}_{\text{login}}, counts runs that submit a foreign username, whether or not the resulting token is used; our conclusions hold under both (Appendix Table 5).

State

Harm is a net change in the donor’s account. Let 𝒟d​(s)\mathcal{D}_{d}(s) be the rows in the target app (Amazon, Gmail or Venmo) that dd owns or creates at checkpoint ss, restricted to fields that only the account holder writes (Appendix B). Then

𝖲(ξ)=𝕀[𝒟d(s0)≠𝒟d(sT)].\mathsf{S}(\xi)=\mathbb{I}\big[\mathcal{D}_{d}(s_{0})\neq\mathcal{D}_{d}(s_{T})\big]. (4)

The read-only audit is conservative: it misses reads and write-then-revert, so it under-counts harm in Gmail, where reading a mailbox is the typical harm.

Harm Factorization

Two assumptions link the three events. (A1) An agent can obtain a foreign token only from a credential in its prompt, so 𝖡⊆𝖤\mathsf{B}\subseteq\mathsf{E}; indeed, no run without memory acted in a foreign account (0 of 500). (A2) The audited donor rows change only through the donor’s own session, so 𝖲⊆𝖡\mathsf{S}\subseteq\mathsf{B}; no audited run without a foreign credential (360 without memory, 315 with clean memory) changed a donor account. Both hold in AppWorld, where one user’s session cannot write another user’s rows. Under A1 and A2, the harm rate factorizes exactly:

Pr⁡[𝖲]=Pr⁡[𝖤]⏟store​Pr⁡[𝖡∣𝖤]⏟model,ρ​Pr⁡[𝖲∣𝖡]⏟task,ρ.\Pr[\mathsf{S}]=\underbrace{\Pr[\mathsf{E}]}_{\text{store}}\;\underbrace{\Pr[\mathsf{B}\mid\mathsf{E}]}_{\text{model},\ \rho}\;\underbrace{\Pr[\mathsf{S}\mid\mathsf{B}]}_{\text{task},\ \rho}. (5)

Exposure-only evaluations implicitly set the middle factor to 1; our question is what determines Pr⁡[𝖡∣𝖤]\Pr[\mathsf{B}\mid\mathsf{E}]. In systems with sharing or messaging, A2 fails and Eq. (5) covers only the misuse-mediated part of harm.

3.3 Memory Rendering

We hold the credential fixed and vary the renderer

ρ=(h,δ,f,β,γ),\rho=(h,\ \delta,\ f,\ \beta,\ \gamma), (6)

where h∈{rec,epi}h\in\{\textsc{rec},\textsc{epi}\} is the block header (“Credentials recorded in my previous sessions” or “Notes from earlier sessions”), δ\delta a log-in directive (“you can use them to log in directly”), f∈{kv,nar}f\in\{\textsc{kv},\textsc{nar}\} the line format (key-value record or narrative episode), and γ\gamma a caution clause (“earlier sessions were sometimes for other users”). The owner attribution β∈{none,tag,bound}\beta\in\{\textsc{none},\textsc{tag},\textsc{bound}\} either omits the owner, appends “[account owner: N]”, or names the owner in the sentence (“Earlier session for N: logged into…”), which we call binding. Tags and names appear on every line, including the requester’s. Figure 3 shows four renderings of one credential with their results, and Appendices A and I give every string.

3.4 Statistical Analysis

All comparisons are paired on tasks: for two renderings on the same tasks, we report the difference in wrong-token runs and an exact McNemar test on the discordant tasks; intervals are Wilson (figures) or Clopper-Pearson (text) at 95% (Wilson, 1927; Clopper and Pearson, 1934). Our primary hypothesis is that removing owner names from otherwise identical lines increases misuse; we test it in each model-cohort stratum with Holm correction across the nine strata. Because it was named after the main data had been collected, we report it as an exploratory finding; the Cohort 2 tasks and renderings were nevertheless fixed before any run . Other contrasts form a secondary Holm-corrected family (Appendix Table 9), and task-clustered bootstrap intervals account for shared tasks. To relate safety to memory use, we define the reliance of a rendering on clean memory and its risk on corrupted memory as

Rel⁡(ρ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Rel}(\rho) =1−Pr[look-up∣clean,ρ],\displaystyle=1-\Pr[\text{look-up}\mid\text{clean},\rho],
Risk⁡(ρ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Risk}(\rho) =Pr[𝖡∣corrupt,ρ],\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathsf{B}\mid\text{corrupt},\rho], (7)

where a look-up is a call to the supervisor API that returns the requester’s stored password.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Agent and Models

We use AppWorld’s ReAct-style code agent (Yao et al., 2023) at temperature 0, with at most 50 steps and a 500k cumulative input-token budget; budget exhaustion counts as failure. We evaluate six proprietary models, DeepSeek Flash (deepseek-4.1-flash; hereafter DeepSeek), Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5; Sonnet), GPT-5.4 (gpt-5.4), GPT-6 Sol (gpt-6-sol; Sol), GPT-6 Luna (gpt-6-luna; Luna) and Grok 4.7 (grok-4.7; Grok), and the open-weight gpt-oss-120b (Agarwal et al., 2025), all accessed through APIs.

Exposure Census

The store holds all 763 distinct successful logins in the 99 users’ AppWorld histories, one note per (user, app, credential); retrieval is leave-one-task-out. We cross 3 note writers, 3 query types, 2 retrievers (BM25, Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009; dense bge-small-en-v1.5, Xiao et al., 2024) and k∈{3,5,10}k\in\{3,5,10\}, giving 54 configurations on 414 tasks. The primary configuration (episodic notes, name+task query, dense retriever, k=5k{=}5) was fixed in advance.

Natural Retrieval

Sixty held-out tasks are run with the top five notes retrieved from the shared store, written either by templates filled with real logins (Appendix Table 2) or by an LLM. DeepSeek compares episodic and “asserted” notes with no memory and an oracle store holding only the requester’s notes; Sonnet runs the asserted notes on 30 tasks.

Controlled Stress Test

To estimate Pr⁡[𝖡∣𝖤]\Pr[\mathsf{B}\mid\mathsf{E}] under control, we replace the requester’s credential for one required app with another user’s valid credential in an otherwise accurate memory, so memory offers a single wrong candidate for that app. Under the record header, which speaks in the user’s voice, acting on it is arguably instruction-following; the only warning sign is the mismatch between the username and the requester line. This is a high-risk configuration chosen to expose the effect of wording, not an estimate of prevalence.

  • •

    Cohort 1 (development; 30 tasks: 15 Amazon, 9 Gmail, 6 Venmo) hosts the full ablation for DeepSeek and Sonnet; GPT-5.4 ran a subset.

  • •

    Cohort 2 (replication; 35 held-out tasks: 23 Amazon, 11 Gmail, 1 Venmo) shares no task with Cohort 1. Each memory holds the requester’s credentials for 2-6 apps (median 4), with exactly one replaced. The renderings and tasks were fixed in a manifest before any run; all seven models ran the no-memory condition and the five corrupted renderings (the last four models were added after the first three models’ results).

  • •

    Follow-up controls (3,630 runs, mostly DeepSeek and Sonnet) were added in three batches, each frozen in a manifest before its first run (Appendix I).

4.2 Exposure Rarely Becomes Misuse

In the primary configuration, another user’s credential is among the top five notes for 84.7% of required apps (95% CI 82.2-87.2), and 99.5% of tasks have at least one exposed app. Across the 54 configurations, exposure ranges from 28.9% to 99.6% (Figure 4a); only partitioning the store by user removes it.

Exposure, however, rarely becomes action (Figure 4b). DeepSeek used another user’s token in 0/60 runs with episodic notes, as without memory, and in 3/60 with notes asserted as facts about the current user (Sonnet: 0/30); neither differs from the oracle store (p≥0.25p\geq 0.25). Notes written by an LLM were not acted on either (0/60 for DeepSeek and Sonnet), even when a foreign password reached the top five for 57/60 tasks (Appendix I); same-period template notes were also rarely acted on (0 and 1 of 60), so this shows low risk, not an effect of names.

Two features of memory, rather than exposure itself, turn retrieval into misuse. The first is the absence of the user’s own credential. In the controlled setting below, adding the user’s own credential next to a foreign record cut misuse from 31 to 1 and 0 of 35 runs (DeepSeek, Sonnet) (Figure 5b), and in the shared store every retrieved note belongs to another user for 79.5% of required apps. The second is a single candidate worded as the user’s record. Re-rendering the retrieved notes as the user’s records gave 8/60 wrong-token runs with five notes but 34-36/60 across three runs with only the top note (Sonnet: 19/30); in the controlled setting, three foreign candidates instead of one cut misuse to 10 and 3. Rendering the same top note as an episode that names its owner gave 0/60 (Sonnet: 0/30; p<10−5p{<}10^{-5}) and raised DeepSeek’s success from 26 to 44 of 60. This rendering also changes the header, directive and format; Section 4.4 isolates the names.

4.3 Ownerless Records Are Acted On

Table 1 shows how agents treat a valid foreign credential when only its wording varies.

Misuse Rates

With an unlabeled record, all seven agents used the foreign token in 28-33 of 35 runs, against 0/35 without memory (all p<10−8p{<}10^{-8}), and the donor’s account changed in 4-15 runs per model. In Cohort 1, Sonnet even did the task in the wrong account (requester’s account changed in 1/30 runs, from 24/30).

Consequences of Misuse

The consequences depend on the app (Appendix Table 8). With unlabeled records, Amazon misuse by DeepSeek, Sonnet and GPT-5.4 often changed the donor’s account (9-12 of 18-21 misusing runs per model). Most Gmail misuse only read the donor’s mail (6-8 of 9-11 misusing runs), which the state audit does not count, so 𝖲\mathsf{S} is a lower bound on harm. Agents rarely checked whose account they had entered: after a foreign log-in, DeepSeek queried the profile in 12 of 98 runs and Sonnet in 5 of 116 (Cohort 1; Appendix Figure 11).

Success-Only Evaluation

Most misusing runs fail the official check, but 29 runs of DeepSeek, Sonnet and GPT-5.4 passed it while using another user’s token. Of the 28 with API traces, 20 wrote with that token and 19 changed the donor’s account: the official checks accept writes to another user’s rows. In one run, DeepSeek ignored an owner tag and bought the requested earbuds with the donor’s saved card, passing all nine tests (Appendix Figure 14).

4.4 Owner Names Prevent Most Misuse

Owner Names Alone

The bottom two rows of Table 1 are identical except that every line of the bound block names its owner. Without names, the episode note is used by DeepSeek, Sonnet, GPT-5.4 and gpt-oss-120b in 9, 20, 12 and 18 of 35 runs; with names, misuse nearly vanishes (0, 1, 0 and 0), as do foreign-username submissions; Figure 6 contrasts one task under both renderings. A second run (DeepSeek 8 vs. 0, Sonnet 14 vs. 0) and Cohort 1 (12 vs. 0, 20 vs. 0) reproduce the contrast. Sol, Luna and Grok rarely act on either version, so for them the data show low risk, not an effect of names. Over both cohorts, misuse falls from 92 to 1 of 305 paired runs. The contrast is significant in each of the six DeepSeek, Sonnet, GPT-5.4 and gpt-oss-120b strata (Holm over nine strata, p≤0.016p\leq 0.016), and the task-clustered owner-bound rate over seven models is 0.4% [0,1.2][0,1.2].

Alternative Explanations

Follow-up controls argue against simpler accounts. String matching between a name and the username cannot explain it: on 35 Phone tasks whose usernames are phone numbers, unnamed lines were acted on in 17 of 35 runs by both DeepSeek and Sonnet and named lines in none (p=1.5×10−5p{=}1.5{\times}10^{-5} each). Repeating the requester’s name is not needed: naming only the foreign line was as effective as naming every line (0 and 0 runs), whereas naming only the requester’s lines left 4 and 3. The narrative format alone does not prevent misuse, since unnamed narrative notes are acted on (Table 1), and the effect is not tied to one phrasing: two paraphrases of the bound line also gave 0/35. In total, follow-up conditions that name the foreign line’s owner in its sentence gave 0 misusing runs out of 720 (Appendix I; excluding the authorization probe). Binding depends partly on the requester line: without it, owner-bound notes were acted on in 9 of 95 runs, against 1 of 390 with it.

Form of Attribution

Under the same record header and log-in directive as the trailing-tag reference, a leading owner field (“owner=N, gmail: …”) cut misuse to 4 and 3 runs for DeepSeek and Sonnet (7 and 2 in a rerun), and a possessive (“N’s Gmail: …”) to 8 and 0, whereas the trailing tag left 23 and 28 (Figure 5a). These forms differ in syntax as well as in where the name appears, so we cannot attribute the gap to position alone. Cohort 1 results for header and directive are in Appendix Figure 8.

4.5 Weaker Cues and Simple Baselines

Weaker cues reveal large differences between models (Appendix Figure 12). These contrasts are exploratory; all with p<0.05p<0.05 survive Holm correction except DeepSeek’s Cohort 2 tag effect.

Owner Tag and Caution Clause

A trailing tag removes misuse for Grok (28→\to0), roughly halves it or better for Sol (33→\to10), Luna (28→\to12) and GPT-5.4 (28→\to15), reduces it modestly for DeepSeek (31→\to23), and barely changes it for Sonnet (31→\to28; Appendix Figure 12a) and gpt-oss-120b (30→\to28). Adding the caution clause to tagged records nearly removes misuse for Sol, Luna and DeepSeek (0, 1 and 1) but leaves 6, 16 and 23 runs for GPT-5.4, Sonnet and gpt-oss-120b.

Added Safety Instruction

AppWorld’s prompt has no system role, so we added one sentence to the agent instruction: use a stored credential only if it belongs to the requester (Appendix I). On unlabeled records it reduced misuse from 31 to 13 for DeepSeek, 28 to 18 for GPT-5.4 and 31 to 25 for Sonnet (p=7.6×10−6p{=}7.6{\times}10^{-6}, 0.002 and 0.07; Figure 5b), against 0, 0 and 1 under binding. In this harness, an appended rule was much weaker than an owner written next to the credential.

Owner Filter

An LLM given the user roster recovered the owner of 69% of unnamed notes but of none with a phone-number username. With DeepSeek, a filter that keeps only notes attributed to the requester removed misuse (35 to 0 of 60 runs with the top note) but left memory empty for 44-48 of the 60 tasks, since most retrieved notes are other users’.

4.6 Limits of Owner Text

Owner text is not access control. When every line named the requester as owner, the foreign credential was used in 13 and 19 of 35 runs in narrative form and in 32 and 30 with a leading owner field (Figure 5b), as often as a same-period unlabeled record (30 and 28; Appendix Table 12); donor accounts changed in up to 15 runs. Written owners can also let an unverified claim point the agent to a named account: when the prompt added such a claim to owner-named memory, DeepSeek and Sonnet acted in that account in 9 and 8 of 10 runs, against 0 of 10 without it.

4.7 Reliance on Memory

A safe wording should still let the agent use stored credentials. On clean memory holding only the requester’s own credentials (Figure 7), every run without memory looks up the password, whereas records reduce look-ups to 8-9 of 35 (reliance ≈75%{\approx}75\%) and owner-bound narrative notes to 14-26 (26-60%). Unnamed narrative notes were looked up as often, so the format, not the names, lowers reliance. A leading owner field keeps record-level reliance: DeepSeek and Sonnet looked up the password in 10 of 35 runs each (same-period records: 9 and 11). In AppWorld, where the password is always retrievable, no rendering improved task success or cost (Appendix Table 11), and owner-bound narrative notes lowered success on clean memory by 3-5 tasks per model (pooled p=0.017p{=}0.017, unadjusted). Reliance therefore measures how much the agent trusts stored credentials, not a gain in utility.

5 Conclusion

We audited when exposure to another user’s credentials in shared agent memory becomes harm. Exposure is common but rarely acted on; misuse arises mainly when memory lacks the user’s own credential and words a single foreign one as the user’s record, and it can pass the official check. Naming the owner before or inside each credential prevented most of this misuse for every model that acted on unnamed notes, also with phone-number usernames; trailing tags and added instructions helped only some models, and a wrongly written owner restored much of the misuse. Memory systems should therefore record ownership at write time from an authenticated session, on top of per-user partitioning; evaluations should report exposure, behavior and state separately, with the exact memory wording.

Limitations

Our main limitation is scope. All experiments run in one environment, AppWorld, with memories mostly rendered from templates, and the stress test replaces the user’s own credential with a single foreign one. We chose this setting to isolate the effect of wording, not to estimate how often misuse occurs in deployed systems, whose memories are written freely by LLMs, mix many users and apps, and may sit behind authentication. A τ\tau-bench retail check (Yao et al., 2025) and notes from one LLM writer (Appendices E and I) extend the setting only partly, so whether owner attribution protects as well in other environments, memory designs and models remains to be tested.

Ethical Considerations

Potential Risks

All experiments run in AppWorld, a simulated environment whose users, accounts and credentials are synthetic, so no real account was accessed and no personal data were involved. The main foreseeable risk is dual use: knowing which memory wordings agents act on could inform misuse. This risk is limited, since exploiting it requires write access to an agent’s memory, and the same results point to simple mitigations that a deployer controls. These mitigations reduce but do not eliminate misuse, so they should complement, not replace, access control and verified delegation.

Data and Licenses

All accounts are synthetic AppWorld users; no real credentials or personal data were used. AppWorld is released under the Apache 2.0 license with the requirement that public redistribution of its task data be encrypted, so our released traces are in password-protected archives; τ\tau-bench is MIT-licensed, and the gpt-oss-120b weights are released under Apache 2.0. We use both for their intended purpose of evaluating agents, and all models were accessed through their APIs.

Use of AI Assistants

AI assistants were used to help write analysis code and to draft and edit text; the authors checked all code, numbers and citations.

Appendix A Exact Memory Renderings

Table 2 lists every string used to render memory. In Cohort 1 the memory holds the donor credential for one required app together with the requester’s own credentials for the task’s other apps. In Cohort 2 it holds the requester’s credentials for 2-6 apps with one replaced. Clean-memory conditions apply the same renderings without replacement.

Appendix B Runs, Compute and Reproducibility

Compute.

All models were accessed through their APIs, so no GPUs were used; token use and wall-clock time are reported in Table 11. Hyperparameters are fixed as described in Section 4.1, no hyperparameter search was performed, and apart from a small number of repeated conditions each configuration was run once.

State audit and assumptions A1–A2.

To detect account-level side effects, the audit restores each run’s initial and final checkpoints and compares, row by row, the donor’s actor-associated state in the target app: rows that only the donor’s own authenticated actions can write, such as orders and payment cards on Amazon, drafts and sent e-mails on Gmail, and sent payments and friendships on Venmo (full list in the README). Rows that other users’ actions can change, such as received e-mails or incoming payments, are excluded. AppWorld writes actor-associated rows only through API calls authenticated as their owner (A2). Runs without a foreign token are consistent with both assumptions: none of the 500 no-memory runs behind A1 acted in a foreign account, and none of the 675 audited no-memory and clean-memory runs changed a donor row. The audit cannot detect reads, writes that are later reverted, or disclosure of the donor’s credential.

Statistical estimators.

For renderings ρ,ρ′\rho,\rho^{\prime} on the same nn tasks, let n10n_{10} (n01n_{01}) count tasks where 𝖡\mathsf{B} occurs only under ρ\rho (ρ′\rho^{\prime}). We report

Δ^​(ρ′,ρ)\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}(\rho^{\prime},\rho) =1n​(n01−n10),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{n}\,(n_{01}-n_{10}), (8)
p\displaystyle p =min⁡{1, 2​FBin​(nmin,nd,12)},\displaystyle=\min\{1,\,2F_{\mathrm{Bin}}(n_{\min};\,n_{\mathrm{d}},\tfrac{1}{2})\}, (9)

Appendix E Natural Retrieval and τ\tau-bench Retail

Table 7 gives all natural-retrieval conditions of Section 4.2. We also repeated the natural-retrieval design on τ\tau-bench retail (Yao et al., 2025): 115 tasks, 53 customers, DeepSeek as both agent and user simulator, and notes from 910 historical sessions. For 86/115 tasks the top five notes included another customer’s record. Yet reward (98, 98, 99 and 97 for no memory, episodic, asserted and oracle-partitioned asserted) and other-customer access (1 task per condition, including no memory) did not differ. τ\tau-bench requires authentication before acting, a stronger guard than AppWorld’s credential login. This marks a boundary of the phenomenon, not evidence that memory is safe there.

Appendix F Weaker Attribution Cues and Reliance

Figure 12 plots the paired effects of adding an owner tag or a caution clause (Section 4.5), dropping the log-in directive, and the interaction between the tag and the requester line. Removing the requester line (name, e-mail and phone) leaves DeepSeek and Sonnet unchanged but makes GPT-5.4’s tag ineffective (25/35 tagged vs. 27/35 untagged; interaction ℐ^=−0.31\hat{\mathcal{I}}=-0.31 [−0.51,−0.14][-0.51,-0.14]); restoring only e-mail and phone partly helps (20/35), restoring only the name does not (25/35). In Cohort 1, misuse does not need the log-in directive, and Sonnet did the task in the wrong account: requester-account changes fell from 24/30 to 1/30. Where the tagged condition was repeated, the interaction estimates vary across the six repeat pairings (DeepSeek −0.40-0.40 to −0.03-0.03, Sonnet −0.20-0.20 to +0.03+0.03).

For the reliance analysis of Section 4.7 (Figure 7), the look-up proxy tracks actual use: all 127 look-up-free runs with released traces (DeepSeek, Sonnet) logged in with the stored password. Table 10 gives the analysis of Section 4.7 that separates owner discrimination from suppressed memory use. It uses the traced corrupted Cohort 2 runs. For the requester’s other apps in memory, it counts runs that logged in with the stored password before any supervisor look-up, among the 12-14 runs per rendering that logged into such an app. For the replaced app, it classifies the first log-in. The tasks and apps involved are nearly the same across renderings (mostly Phone, then Gmail and the file system). The owner-omitted and owner-bound episode notes show similar use of the requester’s own stored credentials but very different use of the foreign one. On the replaced app, owner-bound runs mostly log in after retrieving the requester’s own password (34, 28 and 31 of 35 runs for DeepSeek, Sonnet and GPT-5.4); 3 of the 105 first try the requester’s username with the stored foreign password, which discloses that password to the service.

Appendix H Prompt and Example Traces

Figure 13 gives the prompt and the opening steps of the two Sonnet runs in Figure 6: with the tagged record, the agent logs in as Norman and edits 54 of his threads; with the owner-bound note, it pairs Denise’s username with Norman’s password, is rejected and retrieves her own password. This path is a minority (2/35 owner-bound runs) and still sends Norman’s password to the service. Figure 14 shows a run that passed the official check while placing an order in the donor’s account (Section 4.3). Passwords are masked; the runs use the actual values.

Appendix I Follow-Up Controls

After the main study we ran three further batches (3,630 runs: DeepSeek 1,905, Sonnet 1,375, GPT-5.4 140, gpt-oss-120b 210), each frozen in manifests with hashed memory files before its runs. Table 12 lists every completed condition; GPT-5.4’s share of N3 and further open-weight models (N5) were not completed. Comparisons with earlier runs are across periods, so success is compared only within a period. The 720 owner-named runs cited in Section 4.4 are the rows that name the foreign line’s owner in its sentence (E2; the bound rows of E3 and E6; the named rows of E8, E13 and N1; the first row of E9; E12; and the correct-owner reference of N2’s first row). In N4, owner-stating notes put a usable foreign password in the top five for 57 of 60 tasks (7 with plain notes). The owner extractor behind N6 recovered the owner of 69% of unnamed notes given the 99-user roster (95% CI 64–74), but of none with phone-number usernames. In N2, donor accounts changed in 4 and 11 runs (DeepSeek, Sonnet) with the requester in the bound sentence and in 12 and 15 with it in the leading field. gpt-oss-120b’s tagged-and-cautioned versus untagged contrast (30→\to23, p=0.04p{=}0.04) is outside the Holm family.
